rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Poisson's ratio** σ is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain for a stretched body — a **dimensionless** pure number, because it compares two strains each of which is already length-over-length (NEB 2024). Stretching a wire thins it: with σ ≈ 0.3 for metals, a 0.1% stretch shrinks the diameter by 0.03%.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Definition and Sign Convention:** $\sigma = -( ext{lateral strain})/( ext{longitudinal strain})$. The negative sign makes $\sigma$ positive for ordinary materials (lateral and longitudinal strains have opposite signs). The ratio is dimensionless — dividing one dimensionless strain by another.  ·  **Volume Change Constraint:** The fractional volume change under uniaxial stress is $\Delta V/V = \varepsilon(1 - 2\sigma)$. For $\sigma = 0.5$ (incompressible), $\Delta V/V = 0$ — volume is conserved. For $\sigma < 0.5$, volume increases slightly during stretching.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Remember the minus sign in σ = −(lateral)/(longitudinal) — it makes typical σ positive.  ·  σ is dimensionless — do not attach units.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Wire*** — 0.1% stretch, σ = 0.3 → diameter shrinks 0.03%.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **No units for σ:** strain ÷ strain = pure number.  ·  **Lateral strain is a contraction** — hence the conventional minus sign.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Compute σ from measured lateral and longitudinal strains.  ·  Compute σ from E and G using E = 2G(1+σ).

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Say 'ratio of two strains — hence dimensionless' verbatim."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A wire of diameter 1 mm stretches 0.2% with σ = 0.28. Find ΔD.** — lateral strain = 0.28 × 0.002 = 5.6×10⁻⁴; ΔD = 5.6×10⁻⁴ × 1 mm = 0.00056 mm (decrease).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The 2024 question pairs bulk modulus with Poisson's ratio — prepare both definitions together.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **σ links all three moduli:** Y = 2η(1+σ) = 3K(1−2σ) — only two elastic constants are independent.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: σ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain (dimensionless).  ·  Metals ≈ 0.3; rubber ≈ 0.5; cork ≈ 0; limits −1 to 0.5.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Cork's near-zero Poisson ratio makes it ideal for bottle stoppers — it doesn't bulge when pushed in.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Stretch Here, Shrink There Stretch a rubber band and it visibly thins; stretch a cork and it barely changes width. Poisson's ratio captures this sideways response — the lateral contraction that accompanies every longitudinal stretch — and it is dimensionless because it compares strain with strain.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024) ### 2.1 Definition When a wire is stretched longitudinally, its diameter decreases laterally. **Poisson's ratio (σ)** is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain: $$\sigma = \frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} = \frac{-\Delta D/D}{\Delta L/L}$$ ### 2.2 Why is it dimensionless? (NEB 2024) Both numerator and…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 40:** σ links the three moduli: $Y = 2\eta(1+\sigma) = 3K(1-2\sigma)$. - **To volume conservation:** σ = 0.5 → no volume change on stretching; σ < 0.5 → volume increases slightly. - **To auxetic materials:** σ < 0 (they get *fatter* when stretched) — engineered metamaterials.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Material State Limits:** The thermodynamic bounds are $-1 < \sigma < 0.5$ for isotropic materials. Most common materials have $0 < \sigma < 0.5$. Auxetic materials (negative $\sigma$) expand laterally when stretched — rare and engineered. Fluids have no defined Poisson's ratio (no shear rigidity).  ·  For steel, σ ≈ 0.25–0.3; for rubber, σ ≈ 0.5; for cork, σ ≈ 0.  ·  Volume is conserved when σ = 0.5 (ΔV/V = 0).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB often asks to compute σ using E = 2G(1+σ) given E and G.  ·  Verified PYQ: definition + dimensionless reasoning (2024, 3m).  ·  "Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain."

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Why does a stretched rubber band get visibly thinner while a steel wire barely changes?  ·  Compute the lateral change for a stretched wire given σ and strain.  ·  Show that rubber (σ = 0.5) conserves volume.
